Issued at 323 AM EDT Mon Sep 7 2026

Early this morning model analysis and satellite imagery continued to 
show upper level ridging over the plains states ahead of an upper 
level low over the Pacific Northwest. Shortwave energy was pushing 
over the top of the ridge resulting in areas of showers and 
thunderstorms over northern MN and southern Manitoba. High level 
cloudiness from these storms was streaming southeast into the U.P. 
with the northwest flow aloft. The added cloud cover was keeping 
temperatures warmer than last night, ranging from the 60s in the 
west to the 50s east.

The upper level pattern begins to shift tonight into Tuesday as the 
central CONUS ridge is flattened out by a deep trough lifting out of 
the Pacific Northwest into the Canadian Prairies. This will induce 
surface cyclogenesis in the lee of the northern Rockies on today, 
with a strong low then tracking to the southern shores of Hudson Bay 
by Wednesday morning and driving a strong cold front across the UP 
late Tuesday into early Wednesday.

For today, light winds and above average temperatures are on tap as 
high pressure moving through Ontario continues to keep the area dry. 
More clouds can be expected today though as the upper level low over 
the Pacific Northwest inches closer. Expect highs in the 70s to low 
80s along with comfortable afternoon dewpoints falling into the 50s 
as mixing reaches into the drier air. This will bring afternoon 
humidity down to 30% in the west but with light winds don't expect 
any fire weather concerns.

A warm front will push through the area late tonight into Tuesday 
with deep moisture along and behind the front. This will bring a 
period of warm, moist air advection resulting in showers and 
thunderstorms along and behind the warm front. Instability increases 
with time behind the warm front, with ensemble joint probabilities 
for 30kt shear and 500+ J/kg mucape increase to 80%, sufficient for 
a few strong to severe thunderstorms. However, the best instability 
lags the forcing associated with the warm front and a strong capping 
inversion will be in place through the day Tuesday as 850mb temps 
warm to 16C but moist low level air and clouds prevent strong 
diurnal heating. Thus it may be difficult to get any storm 
development in the lagging, more unstable airmass.

Overall, expect most of the area to receive a wetting rainfall from 
this event as latest NBM has a 65% or greater chance to receive at 
least a quarter inch for a but the far southcentral UP (closer to 
50%) through Tuesday night. The western UP from the Keweenaw to the 
Porcupines has a 40-60% chance to receive an inch or more of rain on 
Tuesday, but those probabilities quickly drop off to 10-25% over the 
central and eastern UP. Rain should depart the eastern UP behind a 
cold front by Wednesday morning. 

This system will also make for breezy conditions from Tuesday into 
Wednesday, with southerly winds increasing to 15-30 mph across a 
wide swath of the area on Tuesday ahead of the front. The strongest 
gusts on Tuesday will be in the areas favored by southerly downslope 
flow, particularly from the Huron Mountains eastward along the Lake 
Superior shoreline. Winds will shift westerly on Wednesday, aided by 
cold air advection and pressure rises behind the front. Expect 
widespread gusts of 20-30 mph through the day, with stronger gusts 
to 40 mph possible near Lake Superior. Will need to consider an 
eventual Wind Advisory for the Keweenaw as NBM now shows a 60-80% 
chance for gusts of 45+ mph there. Meanwhile, there is also a 25-35% 
probability for 45 mph gusts along the shoreline from east of 
Marquette to Whitefish Point.

Expect calmer weather to return to the region by Thursday as high 
pressure temporarily builds back over the UP behind the departing 
system, with highs on Thursday closer to seasonal norms in the mid 
60s to low 70s. However, the overall pattern remains unsettled as 
another trough has the potential to bring additional rounds of 
precipitation and breezy conditions from Friday into the weekend.
